name: Carbon Bonding and Structural Diversity
what: This subtopic examines why carbon forms such a wide variety of stable compounds, focusing on its four valence electrons, the strength and stability of different covalent bonds it forms, and how structural isomers arise. It also introduces the concept of degree of unsaturation.
why: Understanding why carbon is central to organic chemistry allows you to predict the range of structures a molecule can adopt and compare the stability of different bonds, which is foundational for all subsequent work in organic chemistry.

items.title: I can explain why carbon forms four covalent bonds using its valence electron configuration
items.what: Carbon is in group 14 and has four valence electrons in its outer shell. To achieve stability it shares all four electrons, forming four covalent bonds with neighbouring non-metallic atoms.
items.why: This explains why carbon can bond to so many different atoms and to other carbon atoms in chains and rings, creating the enormous structural diversity seen in organic chemistry.
items.example: In methane (CH4), carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, giving carbon a full outer shell of eight electrons.

items.title: I can define bond strength and compare the relative strengths of common covalent bonds in organic molecules
items.what: Bond strength (average bond energy) is the energy in kJ mol⁻¹ required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in the gaseous state. Higher bond energy means a stronger and more stable bond.
items.why: Comparing bond strengths helps predict which bonds in a molecule are most likely to break during a chemical reaction, and why some molecules are more chemically stable than others.
items.example: A C–F bond (485 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger and more stable than a C–I bond (240 kJ mol⁻¹) because fluorine has a smaller atomic radius, resulting in a shorter, stronger bond.

items.title: I can explain the two key trends in average bond energy for carbon bonds
items.what: Bond energy increases as the number of bonds between two atoms increases (C–C < C=C < C≡C). Bond energy decreases as you move down a group in the periodic table for bonds to carbon (C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I).
items.why: These trends allow you to rank bond stability without memorising every individual value, and to explain why longer bonds (formed with larger atoms) are generally weaker and less stable.
items.example: A C=C double bond has a bond energy of 614 kJ mol⁻¹ compared to 347 kJ mol⁻¹ for a C–C single bond, so the double bond requires more energy to break.

items.title: I can identify and distinguish between the three types of structural isomers
items.what: Structural isomers share the same molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are connected. The three types are skeletal isomers (different carbon frameworks), positional isomers (same functional group in different positions) and functional group isomers (different types of functional group).
items.why: Recognising isomerism explains why two compounds with identical molecular formulas can have very different physical and chemical properties, which is important for synthesis and identification work.
items.example: Pentan-1-ol, pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol all have the molecular formula C5H12O but differ in the position of the –OH group, making them positional isomers of each other.

items.title: I can calculate degree of unsaturation from a molecular formula
items.what: Degree of unsaturation (DoU) is calculated using the formula DoU = (2C + 2 + N – H – X) / 2, where C is carbon count, N is nitrogen count, H is hydrogen count and X is halogen count. Each double bond or ring contributes 1 to the DoU.
items.why: Calculating the DoU from a molecular formula lets you quickly determine how many double bonds or rings a molecule contains before you see its structure, which helps with identifying unknown compounds.
items.example: For benzene C6H6: DoU = (2×6 + 2 – 6) / 2 = 4, which accounts for the three double bonds and one ring in its structure.

items.title: I can determine degree of unsaturation by counting double bonds and rings in a structural formula
items.what: When a structure is known, the DoU equals the total number of double bonds (including C=O) plus the number of ring systems present in the molecule.
items.why: This approach acts as a cross-check when both the structure and molecular formula are available, confirming that the structure and formula are consistent with each other.
items.example: A molecule containing one C=C double bond, one C=O group and one cyclic ring has a DoU of 3.
